He means that a computer can model a process without the model being that process. A computational simulation of X brings X into being only if X is itself an algorithm [spya-npjt4j]. His examples: a simulated digestive system digests nothing, and a simulated rainstorm wets nothing. Simulations generally lack "the causal powers and intrinsic properties" of what they simulate [spya-npjt4j]. He also states the converse: that X *can* be simulated computationally does not show that X *is* computational [spya-npjt4j]. This picks up a distinction he set aside earlier, between Turing computation approximating continuous or random processes and those processes actually being Turing computations [spya-gw0hsq].

Note how little the argument claims on its own terms. It does not show that consciousness is non-computational. It shows that whole-brain emulation, however detailed, "already assumes that computational functionalism is true" [spya-pbcr03] (computational functionalism being the view that running the right computation is enough for consciousness). So by itself the argument is a charge of question-begging aimed at upload and emulation arguments. It gets its force from the other three arguments [spya-mtzbbg spya-nv6tp0]. He then turns it into a dilemma. If you need a highly detailed biophysical model, that is evidence that non-Turing properties matter, which weakens the case for the emulation being conscious [spya-tb4wr2 spya-xvm37k]. He applies the same move to Bostrom, whose simulation argument simply assumes that "a computer running a suitable program would be conscious" [spya-xdy4fe].

For the seminar, the obvious pushback: everything turns on whether consciousness belongs with digestion or with arithmetic, since a simulated calculator really does calculate. Seth admits this conditional structure himself [spya-pbcr03], so the rainstorm analogy does no independent work against a functionalist. The article doesn't say so, but this point and the analogy both go back to Searle. Chalmers' reply that some properties are "organizationally invariant" is the standard counter. Seth's real answer is the argument that brains are not computers [spya-p4vmm0], not the simulation point.

For Seth, predictive processing is the bridge between life and consciousness. It is what turns "life matters" from a hunch into the outline of an explanation.

Here is how the argument runs in the article. Perception is the brain's best guess about what is causing its sensory signals, kept in check by prediction errors: the gap between what it expected and what came in [spya-dp8sem]. That is why he calls experience a "controlled hallucination" [spya-xhvztm]. The same guessing produces our sense of self, including "interoceptive inference," meaning the brain's guesses about the body's internal state [spya-hzp9yz]. Predicting something lets you control it, and a brain's first job is to keep its body alive. That explains why emotions and moods feel good or bad rather than neutral [spya-b59nm2 spya-b228ay]. He then traces this prediction-and-regulation down into the chemistry of each cell. He claims a "mathematical line" runs from autopoiesis (a living system constantly rebuilding itself) to Bayesian best-guessing (updating guesses as evidence comes in) [spya-vys3vj].

The key move is next. He insists that in real bodies this error-reduction is "non-algorithmic": a continuous process probably inseparable from the material it runs on, not a program running on meat [spya-da9tvt]. My inference is that this matters because predictive processing is often read as plain computation. If it were, it would support conscious AI rather than undercut it. He reads it the other way.

This sharpens my earlier answer. The article doesn't say so, but Searle's biological naturalism, as I remember it, says brains cause consciousness without naming a mechanism, and it doesn't put life itself at the centre. Seth's summary of it as "properties of life are necessary" [spya-hj5y6s] is arguably his own version. Also, I brought in "free-energy" myself last time. The article never uses that term. Note how careful he is here: he offers only "glimmers" [spya-da9tvt], admits he has no knockdown argument [spya-hj5y6s], and says his other arguments stand even if this one fails [spya-nv6tp0].

Two people have tested this directly, and their results suggest the "programmer" part of Warth's three-way definition matters most when the programmer is a model.

Yusuke Endoh (mame, a core Ruby developer) [ran Claude Code on the same task in 13 languages](https://github.com/mame/ai-coding-lang-bench). Haskell was the slowest, at 99.6s, despite having the fewest lines of code. He concluded that at least for prototyping-scale tasks, Ruby, Python, and JavaScript (not TypeScript) appear to be the best fit for Claude Code. That's the gap you raised with Paul Graham: fewer lines didn't make the language easier for the model. Dan Luu looked at the claim that compact languages save tokens, the chunks of text a model reads and writes, and per [a secondhand summary of his analysis](https://dev.to/trismegistus/whats-the-best-programming-language-for-ai-coding-agents-hint-its-not-what-you-think-3m6p), the dominant factor is how well the AI model knows the language.

My own view: for a model, what feels "natural" may depend mostly on how much of the language it saw in training, not on whether the language's design fits the problem, as Prolog fits expert systems [spya-npnyrb]. If that's so, does the term still tell you anything about languages, or only about training data?

Yes, though not under this name. The author starts by saying he keeps reaching for a term he has "nowhere to link to" [spya-kahxda]. So what follows are close neighbours of the idea, not earlier uses of "effective expressiveness."

**Inside the piece.** The author names two forerunners himself. Alan Perlis's "Turing tarpit" is the point that a language can do everything while making nothing interesting easy [spya-m6u2kp]. Matthias Felleisen's formal account of expressive power is one the author calls "a step toward" his idea, but says it is still about what can be expressed, not how it feels to express it [spya-s79g0v].

**Outside it, from a web search:**

- **Green and Petre, "Cognitive Dimensions of Notations."** These are design principles for programming languages and other notations. They [give people a shared vocabulary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cognitive_dimensions_of_notations) for judging how usable a notation is. One dimension, "closeness of mapping," asks how closely the notation corresponds to the problem domain world. Green and colleagues also rejected the belief that one notation is best for everything, holding instead that [every notation highlights some kinds of information at the cost of obscuring others](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/200086018_Notational_Systems-The_Cognitive_Dimensions_of_Notations_Framework). That is close to the author's claim that effective expressiveness belongs to a language, a problem and a programmer together [spya-vv3pdc].
- **Kenneth Iverson, "Notation as a Tool of Thought"** (his 1979 Turing Award lecture). Iverson argued that a good notation [must allow convenient expression](https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Kenneth_E._Iverson) of the ideas that come straight from a problem, and also of the ones that turn up later as you analyse it. That is essentially the author's "how naturally it lets a programmer express solutions" [spya-h9rqg0].
- **Paul Graham, "Beating the Averages"** (the "Blub paradox"). Graham imagines a programmer who uses a middling language called Blub. That programmer can see what weaker languages lack, but [looking at stronger ones, "he doesn't realize he's looking up"](https://paulgraham.com/avg.html). Blub seems good enough because he thinks in it. This echoes the author's closing point that a language shapes which problems you bother to take on [spya-kud2sc].

My inference is that Graham differs from the author in one way that matters. Graham ranks languages on a single scale from weak to powerful. The author's point is that there is no single scale: a language's fit always depends on the problem and the person [spya-vv3pdc]. Green and Petre's view is the nearest to the author's.

I also searched your saved articles for "expressiveness" and "Turing tarpit" and found nothing, so it looks like you haven't saved anything else on this.

The essay is a shorter version of Seth's paper [Conscious artificial intelligence and biological naturalism](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/behavioral-and-brain-sciences/article/conscious-artificial-intelligence-and-biological-naturalism/C9912A5BE9D806012E3C8B3AF612E39A) in *Behavioral and Brain Sciences*. That journal prints a target paper alongside replies from other researchers, and it lists 50 replies to this one. Most of the pushback lands on two steps.

The first step is the move from "not computation" to "life". Leonard Dung, in [Why I am not a biological naturalist](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/7ECEE0D995CE25EE727ABF0D85C0DEEF), argues that denying biological naturalism does not logically require computational functionalism. Seth's own essay draws a nearby line, between functionalism in general and its computational kind [spya-f0qxnb]. Dung's point is that this leaves room for conscious AI that is neither alive nor a plain algorithm.

The second step is the claim that life's processes are non-computational. Seth says the way real bodies minimise prediction error is "non-computational, or at least non-algorithmic" [spya-da9tvt]. One reply, [Life is inherently computational](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/behavioral-and-brain-sciences/article/abs/life-is-inherently-computational-and-consciousness-probably-is-too-a-commentary-on-conscious-artificial-intelligence-and-biological-naturalism/CFB6A91374384CDD12A9EED39C9C8FB4), agrees that consciousness rests on life but argues he is wrong to frame these processes as non-computational.

Away from journals, the reaction is more mixed. Benjamin Bratton [called it clumsily argued](https://x.com/bratton/status/2011594253026103434), while other readers praised it.

Which step looks shakier to you?

The essay barely compares itself with other theories by name. It never mentions global workspace theory, higher-order theories or integrated information theory (IIT). Instead it aims at an assumption he thinks most of them share: computational functionalism, the idea that running the right computation is enough for consciousness. He calls his biological naturalism "a minority view." He says rival theories are "framed in terms of standard computation-as-we-know-it," generally avoid saying what would be sufficient for consciousness, and assume computational functionalism rather than defend it [spya-qu7j89]. He then concedes this doesn't make them wrong [spya-zajp75]. He also separates functionalism in general, which he accepts as compatible with his view, from the narrower computational version [spya-f0qxnb]. So his quarrel is mainly about substrate, not about which brain mechanisms matter.

His positive story is predictive processing. Experience is "controlled hallucination" [spya-xhvztm]. Emotion and selfhood come from interoceptive inference tied to bodily regulation [spya-hzp9yz spya-b59nm2]. And the whole thing reaches down into self-maintaining metabolism, which he insists is "non-algorithmic" in real brains [spya-da9tvt]. That last claim is a pressure point worth raising. [Butlin, Long et al.'s 2023 report](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/373246089_Consciousness_in_Artificial_Intelligence_Insights_from_the_Science_of_Consciousness) draws its AI consciousness indicators from recurrent processing theory, global workspace theory, computational higher-order theories, and others, and [another summary](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.05528) says the list includes predictive processing, treated computationally. That report concludes that "if computational functionalism is true, conscious AI systems could realistically be built in the near term". My reading is that Seth's essay is an attack on that "if."

One wrinkle the essay leaves out: IIT reaches a similar verdict on AI for different reasons. The Butlin report left IIT out because it is not compatible with computational functionalism. [Tononi and Koch](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4574706/) have claimed that a neuromorphic electronic device with similar connectivity and dynamics to the brain would be conscious, while a human-equivalent emulation of a brain run on a Von Neumann digital computer would not. Seth also treats neuromorphic and other non-standard hardware as open questions [spya-kjfjgm spya-vs0vpj]. The difference is that for IIT what matters is causal structure, while for Seth it is being alive. My inference is that rejecting computational functionalism is less of a minority position than the essay suggests. What really is a minority position is the claim that life is necessary.

For the lab discussion, the longer version is his [Behavioral and Brain Sciences target article](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/behavioral-and-brain-sciences/article/conscious-artificial-intelligence-and-biological-naturalism/C9912A5BE9D806012E3C8B3AF612E39A), which drew fifty commentaries. One [commentary](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/AFFA2DDBAFEBA04FCD0E86F368F5A468) argues that most of his criteria could be satisfied by digital organisms existing within a sufficiently detailed simulation running on Turing computation.

I couldn't find a published IIT reply to this essay. The article never mentions IIT, nothing in your library covers it, and the one web page I tried returned nothing. So what follows is from memory and unchecked.

The article doesn't say so, but my understanding is that IIT's pushback would mostly not be aimed at his conclusion about AI. Tononi and Koch also reject computational functionalism. On their account, consciousness depends on the intrinsic causal structure of the physical hardware, not on the program it runs. So a conventional digital computer would score near zero on integrated information whatever software it runs. Koch has also used the "a simulated storm isn't wet" argument himself. That puts IIT alongside Seth on two of his four arguments: that implementing the right computation isn't enough [spya-wepmnr], and that simulating something isn't producing it [spya-npjt4j spya-pbcr03]. This also means my earlier "closest to none of them" was too flat. On machine consciousness, IIT is probably his nearest ally of the three theories.

My inference is that the real disagreement is over his third argument, that life is necessary [spya-hj5y6s]. IIT ties consciousness to causal structure, not to metabolism or self-maintenance. On that view, neuromorphic hardware with the right physical feedback loops could be conscious without being alive. Seth half-allows this when he says such technologies "might yet be" up to the job [spya-vs0vpj]. IIT would make the further point that his own predictive-processing story, which runs from metabolism to the brain's best guesses about the body [spya-vys3vj spya-da9tvt], explains how experience feels, not what makes a system conscious at all. Note too that his line about other theories simply assuming computational functionalism [spya-qu7j89] doesn't fit IIT. My reading is that it is aimed at theories like global workspace theory.

Still missing: any actual IIT-side commentary on this essay or on the longer academic version of the argument. I believe a longer version appeared in *Behavioral and Brain Sciences* with open peer commentary, but I haven't verified that. If it did, the commentaries would be the place to look.

Seth admits his position is "a minority view" [spya-qu7j89]. The essay builds on his longer paper in [Behavioral and Brain Sciences](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/behavioral-and-brain-sciences/article/conscious-artificial-intelligence-and-biological-naturalism/C9912A5BE9D806012E3C8B3AF612E39A), a journal that publishes replies alongside papers. It drew 50 replies. In one, [Leonard Dung](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/7ECEE0D995CE25EE727ABF0D85C0DEEF) argues that denying biological naturalism does not logically require computational functionalism, and that Seth's case makes the view worth taking seriously but not more plausible than the alternative. In another, two computer scientists [argue](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/00060C2D9A410D00AA8577408697A279) that Seth makes a case for artificial intelligence consciousness.

Dung's point turns on a distinction the essay itself draws. Do you remember how Seth tells functionalism in general apart from computational functionalism [spya-f0qxnb]?

Hint: He calls one "rather liberal" and the other "very specific" [spya-f0qxnb].

I ran two web searches and neither turned up any reviews or replies, so I can't tell you how it has been received. It did win the 2025 Berggruen Prize essay competition [spya-gp3g6s]. Seth himself says his main position is "a minority view" [spya-qu7j89].

To read alongside it, try the views he argues against: Bostrom's simulation paper [spya-xdy4fe] and the call to take AI welfare seriously [spya-epw4h3]. Reception looks further for what others have said about the piece.

He means that a computer running a model of a process does not thereby produce the process. It produces a description of it, with none of the process's own causal powers. His examples: a simulated digestive system digests nothing, and a simulated rainstorm wets nothing [spya-npjt4j]. The key clause is the exception: simulating X brings X into being only "unless X is a computational process (specifically, an algorithm) itself." He also runs the point the other way: the fact that something *can* be simulated does not show that it *is* computational [spya-npjt4j].

For the substrate question, the important thing is that this argument depends on the others. It does not show by itself that consciousness can't run on silicon. It shows that whole-brain emulation, at any level of detail, "already assumes that computational functionalism is true" [spya-pbcr03]. Computational functionalism is the view that running the right computation is enough for consciousness. So the argument moves the burden of proof onto those who expect emulation to produce a mind; it does not settle the question. His own summary says as much: simulation won't give rise to consciousness "unless computational functionalism happens anyway to be true" [spya-mtzbbg]. That sits uneasily with his claim that each line of argument "can stand up by itself" [spya-nv6tp0]. My inference is that it stands alone only as a diagnosis of a hidden assumption, not as an argument against conscious AI.

He then uses it in two ways. First, he sees a dilemma for mind-uploading. If you think a highly detailed biophysical model is needed, that very fact suggests non-Turing properties matter, so the simulation is less likely to contain you [spya-tb4wr2 spya-xvm37k]. Second, he says Bostrom's simulation argument takes the same assumption as given without examining it [spya-xdy4fe].

The article doesn't say so, but the rainstorm example echoes Searle's from his writing on the Chinese Room. And the standard functionalist reply goes straight at Seth's exception clause: consciousness is more like calculating, which a simulation does do, than like wetness. Whether consciousness falls on the algorithmic side of that line is the whole disagreement, and the simulation/instantiation distinction alone doesn't decide it.

For Seth, predictive processing is the link between life and consciousness: it's how he gets from "the brain keeps the body alive" to "that's why experience feels the way it does." He builds it up in steps:

- **Perception is a best guess.** What we consciously see depends on the brain's predictions about what is causing its sensory signals. Those signals mostly report "prediction errors," the gap between what the brain expected and what it got [spya-dp8sem]. He calls experience a "controlled hallucination": the guesses come from inside and are kept in check by the senses [spya-xhvztm]. He also uses this earlier, where he defines human hallucinations as "uncontrolled perceptions" [spya-t29n67].
- **The self is a best guess too.** This includes "interoceptive inference," which means guesses about the body's internal state [spya-hzp9yz].
- **Predicting the body is how you control it.** He says the brain's "primary duty" is keeping the body alive [spya-b59nm2]. That's why emotion and mood feel good or bad, rather than neutral the way vision does [spya-b228ay].
- **It goes all the way down.** He says prediction-error minimization becomes "inseparable" from metabolism. He draws a line from life's self-producing nature (autopoiesis) to the brain's statistical best-guessing [spya-vys3vj].

The key move comes next. He says this process, as real brains and bodies carry it out, is "non-computational, or at least non-algorithmic." It is a continuous process tied to its physical material, not a program [spya-da9tvt]. My inference is that this is the step everything rests on, and the one most open to dispute. Predictive processing is usually written down as maths that can be run on a computer, so Seth needs the living process itself, not the model of it, to be what matters. That links to his separate argument that a simulation of something is not the thing itself [spya-npjt4j].

He hedges all of this. He presents it as "one possibility" [spya-ps0kap] and says he has no knock-down argument [spya-hj5y6s].

A correction to my last answer: the article never mentions the "free-energy tradition" or Karl Friston. That came from my own background knowledge, and I should have said so.

Two findings bear on your test. The [MirrorCode paper, as one of its authors summarised it on Hacker News](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49245936), compared six languages on very long tasks and found little sign of inter-language differences in solve rates, for any model, but successful Python solutions tended to use fewer tokens than average, while successful Ada solutions tended to use more. That fits the author's split: whether a model *can* solve a problem matches the "can it be expressed" sense [spya-s79g0v], and the effort it takes matches effective expressiveness.

Second, a [study of language preferences in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.17181v3) found that models chose Python in 23/40 instances, despite being explicitly suboptimal. My own view: that's a problem for his working definition, "what kinds of problems make me want to reach for it?" [spya-mjc4vw]. A model reaches for Python out of habit from its training, not because Python fits the problem.

For your question, which would you trust more: what a model reaches for, or what it costs the model to succeed?

Yes, people have written about it under other names. The phrase "effective expressiveness" itself looks like the author's own coining: he says he wrote the note because he had "nowhere to link to" [spya-kahxda]. The article already names two forerunners. One is Alan Perlis's "Turing tarpit," a language where anything is possible but nothing interesting is easy [spya-m6u2kp]. The other is Matthias Felleisen's formal account of expressive power. Warth sees Felleisen's account as a step toward his idea, but says it is still about what a language can express, not how expressing it feels [spya-s79g0v]. Here are three more from outside the piece:

- **Kenneth Iverson, "Notation as a Tool of Thought" (1979).** This was his Turing Award lecture. It [argued that better notations would lead people to deeper insights about mathematics](https://www.hillelwayne.com/post/j-notation/). One of his lines comes close to Warth's "how naturally" idea: a good notation must allow ["convenient expression not only of notions arising directly from a problem"](https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Kenneth_E._Iverson), but also of the ones that come up as you analyse and generalise.

- **Thomas Green and Marian Petre, "cognitive dimensions of notations" (1989 onward).** This is a set of [design principles for notations, user interfaces and programming languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cognitive_dimensions_of_notations), meant to judge how easy they are to use. One dimension is "closeness of mapping": how closely the notation matches the problem it describes. Their key claim is the closest match to Warth's view that the answer depends on language, problem and programmer together [spya-vv3pdc]. They hold that [no dimension is evaluative on its own](https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/~afb21/publications/CT2001.pdf) until you know what activity it has to support. They also reject "superlativism," the belief that one notation is best whatever the task. Instead, [every notation highlights some kinds of information, at the cost of obscuring other kinds](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/200086018_Notational_Systems-The_Cognitive_Dimensions_of_Notations_Framework).

- **Paul Graham, the "Blub paradox" ("Beating the Averages," 2001).** Graham used an imaginary language, Blub, to [compare the power of programming languages in a way that goes beyond Turing completeness](http://taggedwiki.zubiaga.org/new_content/b9991ae5192846497d321442c276b404). His point is that you can't see what a more powerful language offers until you think in it. This connects to Warth's closing point, that a language shapes which problems you bother to take on [spya-kud2sc]. My inference is that Graham differs in one important way: he ranks languages on a single power scale, while Warth's definition depends on who is asking and what they're building, so it resists a single ranking.

Nothing in your saved library mentions expressiveness or the Turing tarpit, so there's no link to your own reading here.

The essay is a short version of a longer academic paper that Seth published in *Behavioral and Brain Sciences*, a journal that prints a lead article together with dozens of replies. In that collection, [Seth says](https://x.com/anilkseth/status/2100638156118753334) he got fifty commentaries, and that he remains highly skeptical about the prospects for conscious AI (for silicon digital systems).

Two critics push from different sides. A [LessWrong post](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/kAHar2hrQbykF9Rt7/contra-anil-seth-on-ai-consciousness) argues that biological naturalism may be correct, but the arguments in favor of it aren't nearly strong enough to confidently rule out AI consciousness. A [Substack critic](https://meditationsondigitalminds.substack.com/p/on-anil-seths-conscious-artificial) says something subtler: he already doubted computational functionalism (the view that running the right computation is enough for consciousness). But most of his reasons for thinking AI could be conscious come from views to which Seth devotes little or no attention. The essay itself grants that functionalism in general is wider than the computational kind [spya-f0qxnb].

The second critique hits harder if Seth's case depends on that one opponent. Does it, as you read it?

He barely compares his view with the others directly. The essay names none of the main rival theories (global workspace, higher-order, recurrent processing, integrated information). It sorts them by a different question: whether consciousness depends on computation or on what the system is made of.

**What the essay says.** The one direct comparison is short. He calls biological naturalism a minority view, and says the other theories are framed in terms of standard computation, mostly avoid stating sufficient conditions, and assume computational functionalism (the idea that running the right computation is enough for consciousness) rather than defend it [spya-qu7j89]. He adds at once that this doesn't make them wrong [spya-zajp75]. His key move is to separate functionalism in general from computational functionalism. Dynamical, embodied and analogue accounts count as functionalist too, and he says running the two together has caused confusion [spya-f0qxnb]. So the line he draws is about the physical substrate, and it cuts across the usual taxonomy of theories. He frames his own view as a necessary-but-not-sufficient condition, with no knock-down argument [spya-hj5y6s].

**Where predictive processing sits.** Inside the essay, his positive account is predictive processing [spya-dp8sem spya-xhvztm], but he insists that prediction-error minimisation in real bodies is continuous and non-algorithmic [spya-da9tvt]. Outside the essay, that's a contested reading. The [Butlin et al. 2023 report](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/373246089_Consciousness_in_Artificial_Intelligence_Insights_from_the_Science_of_Consciousness) took computational functionalism as a working hypothesis and turned theories including recurrent processing, global workspace and higher-order theories into computational indicators [summary of its list](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.05528) that also include predictive processing. So the same theory family is read both ways.

**Integrated information theory.** IIT is the closest outside comparison, and the essay doesn't mention it. Butlin et al. left it out [because it is not compatible with computational functionalism](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/373246089_Consciousness_in_Artificial_Intelligence_Insights_from_the_Science_of_Consciousness). From memory and unchecked: IIT also denies consciousness to conventional digital hardware, but because of its causal structure, not because it isn't alive. My inference is that IIT agrees with Seth on today's AI and disagrees on why.

**How it was received.** The longer version, a [*Behavioral and Brain Sciences* target article](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/behavioral-and-brain-sciences/article/conscious-artificial-intelligence-and-biological-naturalism/C9912A5BE9D806012E3C8B3AF612E39A), drew [fifty commentaries](https://hraness.com/reading/anil-seth-bbs-conscious-ai-biological-naturalism-thread). One [commentary argues](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/AFFA2DDBAFEBA04FCD0E86F368F5A468) that most of his criteria, including embodiment, active inference and metabolism, could be met by digital organisms in a detailed enough simulation. That goes straight at the line between simulation and instantiation that his argument depends on [spya-pbcr03].

I didn't find a published rebuttal from IIT proponents. What I found points the other way: Tononi has just co-signed with Seth. In a [19 October 2026 Nature comment](https://aiweekly.co/alerts/seth-block-tononi-ai-isnt-conscious-perhaps-never-will-be), Seth, Ned Block and Giulio Tononi argue that today's models are not candidates for subjective experience, and that current trajectories of AI development are unlikely to produce it. Their third reason rests on two frameworks, integrated information theory and biological naturalism, arguing that today's deep-learning architectures lack the specific wiring, and the specific material properties, that each framework treats as constitutive of experience.

The disagreement is in the reasoning, not the conclusion. A [critical Substack post on the Nature piece](https://travisgilly.substack.com/p/helping-anil-seth-decide-because) points out that in the IIT section the cerebellum and the computer fail for the same reason, and biology plays no part in the verdict. So the paper's third reason holds two theories that disagree about why.

The article doesn't say so, but from memory: IIT makes consciousness depend on a system's intrinsic cause–effect structure (how its physical parts constrain one another), not on being alive. That means neuromorphic hardware with the right feedback wiring could, in principle, be conscious under IIT with no metabolism at all.
